rules.text: Layout tokens store **parameters only**: the step (L-T8), the growth ratio and the range sizes grow over (L-T10), density multipliers, minimum track sizes, aspect ratios. Every size is generated from them.
Generated sizes are never edited by hand; CI fails if a generated file differs from what the parameters produce.

The fluid range is **320px to 1440px**, measured on the inline size of the nearest query container (L-C1). Outside it sizes stop changing: above 1440px each layout decides how it uses the extra space; below 320px sizes keep their minimum and the content wraps, folds away or changes form (L-R6).
Stored dimensions use the DTCG `dimension` shape, `{ "value": n, "unit": "px" | "rem" }`. The fluid `clamp()` expressions exist only in generated CSS.
Layout tokens are registered with `@property` (type `<length>`, `<number>` or `<ratio>`), so an invalid value is rejected by CSS itself.
**1rem**, the root element's font size, is 16px by default. Tokens are written in `rem`; 16px is only used to convert design values.
The root font size is never set in `px`. If `html` sets a font size at all, it is `100%`, so a user's browser font-size setting still scales the whole interface.
The spacing step is **0.25rem (4px at the default size)**. Every spacing value, gap, padding and control height is a whole multiple of it, after density is applied and before rounding.

Spacing is a curated set of **9 sizes, numbered 1 to 9** from the smallest (`size.1` to `size.9`), not open multiples. Only these sizes can be used. The space between paragraphs is the one exception: it follows the text's line box (T-P2).

All 9 sizes are generated by **one formula** from the same parameters (the 0.25rem step, a growth ratio of **1.5** (the largest size at 1440px is 1.5× what it is at 320px), the 320–1440px range of the nearest query container (L-T3)). Growth scales with the size, so small sizes barely change and large sizes grow most. There are no fixed exceptions. Results are rounded to the 0.25rem step.

Usage names are the CSS properties a size feeds: `gap`, `row-gap` and `column-gap` between elements, `margin-block` and `margin-inline` around one, `padding-block` and `padding-inline` inside one. Each points to a size (`size.1` to `size.9`) or, inside a component, to a ratio (L-T17); it never holds its own value.
Density never adds or removes sizes; it changes the relations between them (L-D1).

**rem owns the system, em owns the inside of a component, and inline-axis spacing between components stays fixed.** rem: font sizes, the 9 sizes, block-axis spacing between components (`row-gap`, `margin-block`), layout tracks, container thresholds, minimum sizes. px: inline-axis spacing between components (`column-gap`, `margin-inline`), generated from the same 9 sizes at 16px to 1rem, so it does not grow with the browser's font-size setting. em: block and inline padding, icon size beside text, icon-to-label gap.

The bridge from rem to em is a set of **unitless ratio tokens** (e.g. block padding = ratio × the component's own font size × density). A component's padding is a relation to its own font size, which is set in rem.
`em` is used only **one level deep**, on a component's own properties. Nested parts take their size from a rem token, never from a chain of ems, so sizes can't compound.

**No raw px values are stored anywhere, including accessibility minimums.** A minimum is a multiple of the 0.25rem step, stored as an alias under the conformance level: target minimum = 6 steps in AA, 11 steps in AAA. At the default font size these equal 24px and 44px.
A minimum is applied inside the formula (`max(value, minimum)`), so a size can never be generated below it. A checker never patches a value afterwards.

Minimums follow the user's browser text size, because they are in `rem`. If a user deliberately sets text smaller than 16px, the minimum shrinks with it; we respect that choice and add no px safety value. CI tests minimums at the default 16px and at larger text sizes.

Names are standard and global: any developer or agent must read a name as the standard term, with no glossary. They come from the DOM, HTML, CSS, ARIA and Angular, never from another design system, because an agent that meets an ambiguous name assumes a meaning and acts on it. A name is invented only where no standard one exists, and a standard term is never reused for something else: in CSS a canvas is the infinite rendering surface, a container is a query container (what frames a component is always written component container), and an inset is the offset of a positioned box.

Layout tokens sit in three groups. `size`: the nine sizes, `size.1` to `size.9`, and the parameters that generate them: `size.step` (L-T8), `size.growth-ratio` (L-T10), and `size.range-start` and `size.range-end` (L-T3). `spacing`: the white space outside and inside elements, each token named after the CSS property it feeds (`gap`, `row-gap`, `column-gap`, `margin-block`, `margin-inline`, `padding-block`, `padding-inline`). `layout`: what divides the space, also named after the CSS property it feeds (`min-inline-size`, `max-inline-size`, `aspect-ratio`).

Every fluid `clamp()` mixes `rem` with a viewport or container unit in its middle term; viewport-only or container-only sizing is not allowed. Inline-axis spacing between components mixes `px` instead (L-T13).
For fluid **text**, the largest size is at most **2.5×** the smallest, so text still reaches 200% under zoom.
Generated sizes are rounded to the 0.25rem step with `round()`, so no layout value lands on a fraction of a pixel.
Every fluid size is tested at 200% and 400% browser zoom on the docs site.

Fluid sizes inside components read the nearest query container through container query units (`cqi`), never viewport units (`vw`, `vi`). With no query container, container units fall back to the small viewport size.
Component styles contain **no viewport `@media` width or height queries**. Components respond to their container with `@container`.
There are no named breakpoints. A layout switch happens at a **calculated threshold**, the sum of the minimum track sizes involved, never at a device number.
Flexible grid tracks use `minmax(0, 1fr)`, not bare `1fr`, so long content can't force a track wider than its container.
Flex and grid children that hold text set `min-width: 0` (or `min-inline-size: 0`) so long words wrap instead of overflowing.
Space between siblings comes only from `gap` with a spacing token. No margins between items inside a primitive.
Only logical properties and values are used (`margin-inline-start`, `inset-inline-end`, `inline-size`…); physical ones (`left`, `margin-right`, `width` for inline sizing) are rejected by lint.
Use grid when the container sets the structure, and flexbox when the content sets the size along one axis.
Full-height surfaces use `dvh` (or `svh` / `lvh`), never `100vh`, so mobile browser bars don't cut off content.
Edge-to-edge surfaces add `env(safe-area-inset-*)` to their padding.
Related elements sit closer together than unrelated ones: the gap inside a group is smaller than the gap around it.

Everything is measured on its **nearest query container**; the viewport is only the top-level case. An element is measured by the container it sits in, never by itself, so everything inside a pane reacts to that pane as it is resized.
Every container has a **minimum and a maximum** inline size. Each is a token, never a raw px value (L-T14).
In-flow containers **push** each other: the one taking space grows to its own maximum first, then its neighbours resize along the split direction.

A container that reaches its minimum reacts as **its component defines**: it freezes its size, minimizes, or reacts in a way specific to that component. Layout never chooses a component's collapsed form.

When containers at their minimum still leave too little room, the **lowest-priority** container gives way: it collapses, minimizes or moves out. Priority follows each pane's importance and frequency of use, per view or task.

Layout only shares space between in-flow containers; it sets no visual traits. Surface, border, corner radius, elevation, stacking order, overlays and padding belong to the **component container**: the system sets whether one opens as an overlay by default and the user controls some views, and its padding uses layout's padding relation, a ratio of the component's own font size (L-T13, L-T17).

Each container takes either the **stretch-fit** size, all the space it is given, or the **fit-content** size, what its content needs. Stretch-fit is reached through grid and flex layout, not the `stretch` keyword, which isn't Baseline.

Three sizes are kept apart: the **content** (for example an icon glyph), the **box** that holds it (the icon box, so every icon aligns the same way), and the **target**, the area that accepts the pointer. The target may be larger than the visible box and transparent. Minimum sizes (L-T14, L-D2) apply to the target.

A target meets a minimum size only when a solid square of that size, aligned to the axes, fits completely inside it. A rounded or clipped target can therefore be undersized, and overlapping target areas don't count.
Layout doesn't decide how a long label behaves (each component's profile says whether it wraps or truncates), nor line height, diacritics and font metrics, which belong to typography.

A single-line control's content area is at least one line box (`1lh`) high, plus its block padding, and its target never goes below the minimum (L-C11), so an icon-only control is as tall as one with text. Multi-line controls declare a minimum and a maximum number of lines.
The `order` property and `row-reverse` / `column-reverse` are not used on content.
Grid placement never puts items in a visual order that differs from the source order.
`reading-flow` is not relied on, because it isn't Baseline.

The layout foundation's primitives are CSS layout mechanisms, named as CSS names them: **flex column**, **flex row** (which wraps item by item, or all at once at a calculated threshold), **grid**, **scroll container** and **aspect-ratio box**. A compound built from them, such as a sidebar, is not part of the foundation layer.
Components and generated pages compose primitives; they don't write their own layout CSS for something a primitive covers.
Each primitive takes only token parameters (a size, a minimum size, a ratio, a threshold), never raw values.
Every primitive is a query container (`container-type: inline-size`) so its children can respond to it.
A **scroll container** that scrolls along the inline axis is keyboard-focusable, has an accessible name, and uses scroll snap.
An **aspect-ratio box** sets `aspect-ratio` from a ratio token, so space is reserved before media loads.
A block of text is about 65 characters wide at most by default, and never more than 80 characters wide in the AAA theme, set with `max-inline-size`.

Media in a stretch-fit container crops to the available area and keeps its aspect-ratio token: `object-fit: cover`, with `object-position` for the focal point. It is never distorted: `object-fit: fill`, the initial value, is not used on media. Static images use `NgOptimizedImage` in fill mode.
The page layout exposes its regions as landmarks: `banner`, `navigation`, `main` (exactly one), `complementary` where used, `contentinfo`.
The page's first focusable element is a skip link to `main`.
Sticky headers and footers set `scroll-padding` to their own size, so focused elements are never covered (fully covered in AA, partly covered in AAA).
The navigation changes form (side navigation to menu button) at a calculated threshold: navigation minimum width plus content minimum width.
The page layout never locks orientation.
On foldables, the page layout may use viewport segments to keep content off the hinge, behind `@supports` only. Without them, the container layout still works.
Density is **two settings**, usable together: **layout density**, the spacing between elements, and **component density**, the spacing inside components.

Density levels are named by the amount of density: **`normal`**, **`more`** for denser and **`less`** for looser. A default is not a level: it is the level in effect when nobody has chosen, set by us per component, or by the system or the device (L-D3).
Density levels are ratios: **`more` 0.75, `normal` 1, `less` 1.25**.
One density applies to a whole page or scope; densities are never mixed inside one hierarchy.
The user's chosen density is stored and always wins over tenant and device defaults.

Layout density scales the gaps between elements and adjusts the growth ratio (the denser the level, the less sizes grow). Component density scales **block padding and control height only**; inline padding and icon-to-label gaps don't change.
Each component's profile says whether density applies to it.
In the AAA level the density `more` is not available.
Component density `more` is never combined with layout density `more`: the denser the components, the looser the spacing between them, so groups stay easy to tell apart.

No density setting can make an interactive target smaller than the **target-minimum alias** for the active conformance level (L-T14). CI verifies the computed result is at least 24 × 24 CSS px (AA) or 44 × 44 CSS px (AAA).
When the user's main pointer is coarse (`pointer: coarse`), the default density is `less`.
When the user asks for more contrast (`prefers-contrast: more`), the AAA theme is selected by default.
An explicit choice by the user or tenant always overrides these defaults.
Nothing is reachable only on hover; every hover affordance also works by focus and by tap.
At 320 CSS px wide, no page scrolls sideways. Only data tables, code blocks and diagrams may scroll, each inside its own scroll container.
Layouts survive the WCAG 1.4.12 text-spacing overrides (line height 1.5, paragraph spacing 2×, letter spacing 0.12em, word spacing 0.16em) with no clipped or overlapping text.
Every layout is tested in both `dir="ltr"` and `dir="rtl"`, with mixed-direction content.
Direction-specific styling uses `:dir(rtl)` / `:dir(ltr)`, not `[dir]` attribute selectors.
Docs-site pages keep Cumulative Layout Shift at or below 0.1.

Nothing becomes unreachable when a layout hides or folds elements away in a small space. A large component that can't work there changes form instead: for example, a table becomes data cards with nested listing and search, with interactions that fit the device, its targets and its readable area.
When a component changes form (L-R6), the new form is functionally equivalent: it offers the same function and the same information, and one kind of component is never swapped for another kind.
Core layout uses only Baseline features (newly or widely available).
Any non-Baseline feature sits inside `@supports`, and the layout still works without it.
